segments.t: The story jumps back to Sapporo in 1980. Instead of making door-to-door sales calls, Toru Muranishi is killing time inside a noisy coffeehouse arcade. When schoolboys start shouting over a tabletop video game, Muranishi snaps at them. Listen to the rough, casual speech first.
いつまでやってんだ！
もう少しでハイスコアだったのに！
お前、どこだ？
北高だ。
そっちこそどこだ！
西中だ！
うるさいな、外でやれ！
外ではゲームできないだろう。
こっちはまだ終わっていない。
痛い！
行くぞ！
ここは札幌の喫茶店だぞ。
Teenagers arguing over an arcade machine drop almost every polite ending. Let's unpack what they are shouting.
いつまでやってんだ！

'How long are you going to keep playing!' "Itsu" means when, and adding "made" stretches it into 'until when' or 'how long'. At the end, "yatte nda" squeezes "yatte iru no da", 'are you doing it', into fast street talk.
もう少しでハイスコアだったのに！

'I almost had the high score!' "Mou sukoshi de" literally says 'with a little bit more', the go-to chunk for 'almost'. Trailing off with "noni" lets frustration hang in the air—'even though I was so close!'
お前、どこだ？
'Where are you from?' Rough "omae" points straight at 'you' among boys picking a fight—never use it with strangers in real life. "Doko da" simply asks 'where is it?', leaving 'your school' unspoken.
北高だ。
'Kita High.' "Kita" means north, and "kou" shortens "koukou", high school, just as "Nishi" means west in the rival boy's answer.
そっちこそどこだ！
'Where are you from yourself!' Putting "koso" right after "socchi", your side, bounces the question right back—'you are the one who should answer!'
うるさいな、外でやれ！
'Shut up, take it outside!' Muranishi barks "urusai", noisy or annoying, softened only slightly by grumbling "na". Then "soto de yare" puts "soto", outside, before the blunt command "yare", do it!
外ではゲームできないだろう。
'We cannot play the game outside, obviously.' "Soto de wa" contrasts 'outdoors' with inside the cafe. "Dekinai" means cannot do, and "darou" nudges the listener with 'right?' or 'obviously'.
こっちはまだ終わっていない。
'I am not finished over here yet.' Pairing "mada", still or yet, with negative "owatte inai", has not ended, gives you the natural Japanese pattern for 'not finished yet'.
痛い！
'Ouch!' One word, "itai", covers both 'it hurts' as a description and 'ouch!' as a sudden cry when somebody bumps you.
行くぞ！
'Here we go!' "Iku", to go, plus tough masculine "zo" turns a plain statement into a rallying shout.
ここは札幌の喫茶店だぞ。

'This is a coffeehouse in Sapporo, you know.' "Koko" points to right here, and "kissaten" is a traditional Japanese coffee shop where salarymen linger over coffee. Now let's hear the whole arcade argument play out again.
いつまでやってんだ！
もう少しでハイスコアだったのに！
お前、どこだ？
北高だ。
そっちこそどこだ！
西中だ！
うるさいな、外でやれ！
外ではゲームできないだろう。
こっちはまだ終わっていない。
痛い！
行くぞ！
ここは札幌の喫茶店だぞ。

Notice the contrast between polite studio Japanese in scene one and blunt street talk here: "itsu made" for 'until when', "mada" with a negative for 'not yet', and "itai" whenever something hurts. See you in the next scene.
じゃあね。
